title: Work and jobs (Beruf und Arbeit)
summary: Say what you do, where you work and what you study, and ask others the same.
goals: Say your job and where you work
Use arbeiten and machen in every person
Use male and female job names (-in)

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1, chapter 9: Working life (Ich bin Lehrerin, Mein Beruf)

sections.title: Talking about work
sections.text:
- [[Was sind Sie von Beruf?]] or [[Was machst du beruflich?]] - What do you do?
- [[Ich bin Entwickler.]] - I'm a developer.
- [[Ich arbeite als Entwickler.]] - I work as a developer.
- [[Ich arbeite bei Siemens.]] - I work at Siemens.
- [[Ich studiere Informatik.]] - I study computer science.

[[bei]] + company, [[in]] + city: [[Ich arbeite bei Siemens in München.]]

sections.title: No 'a' before jobs
sections.text: German says [[Ich bin Entwickler.]] with no article, where English says 'I am **a** developer'. Russian works the same way (Я программист), so this one is easy for you.

sections.title: Male and female job names
sections.text:
Most job names have a female form with **-in**:

- [[der Entwickler]] - [[die Entwicklerin]]
- [[der Lehrer]] - [[die Lehrerin]]
- [[der Student]] - [[die Studentin]]

The plural of the -in forms ends in **-innen**: [[die Lehrerinnen]]. In job ads you will also see forms like 'Entwickler (m/w/d)', which means the job is open to everyone.
Verbs whose stem ends in **t** or **d** add an extra **e** so you can pronounce them: [[du arbeitest]], [[er arbeitet]] (not 'arbeitst', 'arbeitt'). Same for [[antworten]]: [[du antwortest]].

sections.title: In tech
sections.text: In Munich tech companies, English job titles are normal German: 'Ich arbeite als Data Scientist' or 'Ich bin Software Engineer' are perfectly fine sentences.
